title: Build a Portfolio
learningObjective: Apply ownership, lending, pooled investing, risk, time horizon, and cash-access concepts to build a portfolio suited to a long-term goal.
primaryMisconception: A strong portfolio is simply the one with the highest possible growth potential.
secondaryMisconceptions: Every investor should choose the same portfolio.
Holding several individual stocks always creates a diversified portfolio.
Cash has no useful role because it does not usually offer high growth.
A company that does not pay dividends is automatically a poor investment.
keyTakeaway: A strong portfolio fits the goal, timeline, cash needs, diversification, and ability to accept risk.

conceptsAssessed.concept: Investing for a longer-term goal while accepting uncertainty.
Stocks represent partial ownership in companies.
Market prices may move and concentrated stock exposure can be difficult to tolerate.
Mutual funds pool money into professionally managed investments.
ETFs are tradeable baskets that may hold many investments.
Bonds generally represent lending rather than ownership.
Companies may pay dividends or use profit in other reasonable ways.

overview.summary: The learner builds a Rs. 100,000 portfolio for a five-year goal. First, they describe the goal timeline, reaction to a possible decline, and need for accessible cash. Next, they allocate money across stocks, bonds, a mutual fund, an ETF, and cash. They then explain each asset’s role and predict how a company may use profit. The final portfolio check responds to the learner’s earlier profile and allocation. Results measure concentration, access, risk, alignment, understanding, and decision quality—not luck.

screens.title: One Goal, Five Choices
screens.content: You have Rs. 100,000 for a long-term goal. How will you balance growth, price movement, diversification, and accessible cash?
screens.illustration: Five empty portfolio sections surround a Rs. 100,000 allocation meter.

screens.title: The Goal Is Five Years Away
screens.content: Your Rs. 100,000 is for a goal expected in about five years. Basic emergency savings are held separately.
screens.illustration: A five-year goal marker appears beside a separate emergency-savings shield.

screens.title: Prices May Move
screens.content: The portfolio may rise or fall during the five years. You must decide how much movement you could realistically tolerate.
screens.illustration: A portfolio line moves up and down before reaching a five-year goal marker.

screens.title: Access Still Matters
screens.content: Part of the money may need to stay easy to reach. Cash can provide access even when it offers less growth potential.
screens.illustration: A cash pocket sits beside investment baskets and a five-year goal.

screens.title: What Makes a Portfolio Strong?
screens.question: Which approach sounds most balanced before you know the exact allocation?

options.label: Choose only the assets with the highest growth potential
options.feedback: Higher growth potential usually brings more uncertainty and may not fit the goal or cash needs.

options.label: Match the portfolio to the goal, timeline, risk, and cash needs
options.feedback: Correct. A strong portfolio is judged by fit, not by one growth number.

options.label: Use every asset type equally
options.feedback: Using every category equally may ignore the goal and the reason each asset is included.

options.label: Keep everything in cash for every goal
options.feedback: Cash supports access, but a large long-term cash position may limit growth and lose purchasing power.

screens.connectionToSimulation: The next stages test how the portfolio fits the learner’s own selected timeline, reaction, and access needs.

stages.title: Investor Profile
stages.situation: Before allocating the Rs. 100,000, answer three simple questions about when the money may be needed, how a 20% decline might feel, and how much should remain accessible.
stages.objective: Create an educational profile that guides later feedback without producing a formal suitability label.

nodes.question: When might the portfolio money be needed?

choices.label: Within one year
In two to five years
More than five years from now
I am not sure

nodes.question: How might you react if the portfolio fell 20%?

choices.label: Sell everything immediately
Feel worried but review the plan
Accept it as long-term uncertainty
I do not know

nodes.question: Do you need quick access to some of the Rs. 100,000?

choices.label: Yes, a large part may be needed soon
Yes, a small amount should stay accessible
No, most can remain invested
I am not sure

nodes.title: Profile Considerations Ready
nodes.content: These answers guide educational feedback. They are not a professional risk label or personalised recommendation.

feedbackRules.message: More money may need to remain accessible and less exposed to sharp price movement.
A longer timeline may allow more time for price changes, but losses remain possible.
A concentrated stock portfolio may be emotionally difficult to maintain during declines.
A meaningful cash allocation may be useful because selling investments at the wrong time can create pressure.
Uncertainty is useful information. A more moderate starting allocation may be easier to review.

choices.label: Complete all three profile questions honestly
choices.immediateFeedback: The portfolio builder can now compare the allocation with the selected timeline, reaction, and cash needs.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Profile considerations appear beside the builder.
choices.laterConsequence: Alignment, access, and concentration feedback becomes context-sensitive.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Choose the answers that best describe the fictional situation rather than choosing the option that sounds most adventurous.
reasonableAlternatives: A shorter timeline may justify more cash or lower-movement holdings.
A longer timeline may support more growth exposure when possible losses are acceptable.
An unsure learner may reasonably begin with a moderate spread and review it later.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: More growth exposure may increase price movement, while more cash improves access but usually lowers growth potential.

validation.method: Require one response for each of the three questions.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Complete all three profile questions before building the portfolio.
validation.retryBehaviour: Allow answers to be revised until the portfolio allocation is confirmed.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present one labelled question at a time with Previous and Next controls.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Choose one response for the timeline, decline reaction, and access need.

stages.title: Portfolio Builder
stages.situation: Your profile answers are now visible. Divide the full Rs. 100,000 between individual stocks, bonds, a mutual fund, an ETF, and cash. Every allocation changes access, concentration, growth potential, and illustrative risk.
stages.objective: Create a complete portfolio and review how well it fits the selected profile considerations.

educationalAssumptions: Emergency savings are held separately from the Rs. 100,000 portfolio amount.
No real stock, bond, mutual fund, ETF, or provider is named.
Growth potential and risk are educational estimates, not predictions.
Diversification may reduce dependence on one outcome but cannot eliminate loss.
Cash is accessible but may lose purchasing power over time.
Using every category is not automatically better.
The portfolio is judged against the learner’s Stage 1 answers.

examplePortfolios.label: More Spread Out

examplePortfolios.label: High Cash Position

stages.title: Explain the Portfolio
stages.situation: Your portfolio is built. Before judging it, match each holding to its financial role. Understanding the contents matters more than using every category.
stages.objective: Match all five asset types to the role they play inside a portfolio.

rightSideItems.label: Money lent to a company or government
A professionally managed pool of investments
Accessible money that may lose purchasing power

incorrectMatchFeedback.message: Buying a stock generally makes you a partial owner, not a lender.
Buying a bond generally means lending money rather than owning part of the borrower.
A mutual fund may hold many investments using money pooled from several investors.
An ETF is usually a basket containing several investments.
Cash is accessible, but its purchasing power may fall when prices rise.

choices.label: Complete all five matches
choices.immediateFeedback: Understanding what each asset represents helps explain why it was included.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The portfolio understanding score increases by up to 20 points.
choices.laterConsequence: The final dashboard separates allocation from understanding.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Match each asset by its financial role rather than by whether its price may rise.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Two assets may both support a portfolio while creating different ownership, lending, access, and management relationships.

validation.method: Require all five pairs and award four points for each correct match.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: Review whether the asset represents ownership, lending, pooled investing, a tradeable basket, or accessible cash.
validation.retryBehaviour: Keep correct pairs locked and return only incorrect matches with one teaching hint.

stages.title: Company Profit Decision
stages.situation: A company held directly or inside a fund earns a profit. Predict the trade-offs of four profit choices. Then use your profile and current allocation to decide whether the portfolio needs one final adjustment.
stages.objective: Understand that dividends are optional and complete a context-sensitive final portfolio check.

predictionOptions.label: Eligible shareholders may receive cash, while the company keeps less for other uses

predictionCards.explanation: A dividend may provide shareholder cash, but it leaves less money for expansion, debt repayment, or reserves.

predictionOptions.label: The company may expand, but the growth result is uncertain
Shareholders must receive an immediate payment
The company can no longer lose money

predictionCards.explanation: Reinvestment may support products, workers, or expansion, but useful growth and future returns are not guaranteed.

predictionOptions.label: The company may lower what it owes, leaving less for dividends or expansion
Shareholders immediately own a larger percentage

predictionCards.explanation: Debt repayment may strengthen the company, but other uses of profit receive less money.

predictionOptions.label: The company gains flexibility, but too much unused cash may limit growth
The cash guarantees a dividend later
The cash cannot lose purchasing power

predictionCards.explanation: Cash reserves can support emergencies or opportunities, but holding too much unused cash can have a trade-off.

config.importantClarification: There is no single correct use of company profit. The strongest choice depends on debt, growth opportunities, cash needs, risks, and strategy.

finalPortfolioCheck.question: What should happen before the portfolio begins its five-year journey?

choices.label: Keep the portfolio and schedule a later review
choices.immediateFeedback: Keeping the allocation may be reasonable when it already matches the timeline, access needs, and concentration limits.
choices.laterConsequence: The learner must still accept that values can rise or fall.

choices.label: Reduce the largest allocation by Rs. 10,000 and spread it elsewhere
choices.immediateFeedback: This reduces dependence on the largest category when concentration is high.
choices.shortTermConsequence: The largest allocation falls and another suitable category increases.
choices.laterConsequence: Concentration may improve, but losses remain possible.

choices.label: Move Rs. 10,000 from investments to cash
choices.immediateFeedback: This improves access when the current cash allocation does not match the selected need.
choices.shortTermConsequence: Cash rises by Rs. 10,000 and growth exposure falls.
choices.laterConsequence: The portfolio may be easier to use for a near-term need but may have lower growth potential.

choices.label: Move all bonds and cash into individual stocks for maximum growth potential
choices.immediateFeedback: The portfolio chases growth by increasing concentration and reducing accessible money.
choices.laterConsequence: A decline may be harder to tolerate and cash may be unavailable when needed.

recommendedDecisionLogic.strongestApproach: Use the portfolio’s actual mismatch: reduce concentration, improve cash access, or keep the allocation when it already fits.
reasonableAlternatives: Keeping the portfolio is reasonable when no major mismatch appears.
Reducing concentration is reasonable when one category dominates.
Increasing cash is reasonable when the learner expects to need money soon.
recommendedDecisionLogic.tradeOff: Improving access or reducing concentration may lower growth potential, while chasing growth may create a harder portfolio to maintain.

validation.method: Score all four predictions, apply one final portfolio action, and recalculate concentration, cash, growth, risk, and alignment.
validation.invalidStateFeedback: That adjustment cannot be completed because the selected source allocation is below Rs. 10,000.
validation.retryBehaviour: Keep correct predictions. Allow another final adjustment when the chosen source does not contain Rs. 10,000.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Use labelled prediction buttons, then present final adjustment choices with current portfolio metrics.
accessibilityAlternative.instruction: Choose one likely effect for each company decision, then select one portfolio action.

finalChallenge.title: Final Portfolio Check
finalChallenge.situation: After explaining the holdings and predicting company profit choices, the learner must keep or adjust the portfolio using the actual timeline, cash need, and concentration metrics.
finalChallenge.recommendedReasoning: Use the actual mismatch rather than chasing one ideal allocation. Keep a fitting portfolio, reduce concentration, or improve cash access as the situation requires.

debrief.title: Fit Matters More Than Maximum Growth
debrief.content: You built a portfolio by connecting the goal timeline, possible price movement, cash access, diversification, and the role of each holding. Individual stocks represent ownership, bonds represent lending, and funds or ETFs may spread money across many investments. Cash can support access even when its growth potential is lower. You also saw that companies may pay dividends, reinvest, repay debt, or keep cash; no single choice is always best. A strong portfolio is not the one with the highest possible growth. It is the one whose risks, access, and structure fit the goal and can be understood and reviewed.
debrief.simpleSummary: Build for the goal, understand every holding, and avoid unnecessary concentration.
debrief.illustration: A goal, timeline, cash pocket, and five asset cards connect into one balanced portfolio map.

dimensions.label: Profile Awareness
positiveRules: 15 points for completing all three questions and using the answers during allocation review.
10 points when one or more answers are unsure but the final portfolio uses moderate assumptions.
5 points when the learner ignores the selected profile during later choices.
deductions: Deduct 5 when the final action directly conflicts with both timeline and access need.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: This measures whether the portfolio begins with the goal, timeline, reaction, and cash needs.

dimensions.label: Time-Horizon and Cash Alignment
positiveRules: 25 points for strong timeline and access alignment after the final adjustment.
18 points for partial alignment with one manageable mismatch.
10 points for a valid portfolio with a major timeline or access warning.
0 points for increasing the mismatch during the final adjustment.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: This measures whether the money is invested in a way that fits when it may be needed.

dimensions.label: Diversification and Concentration
positiveRules: 25 points for a broadly spread, context-appropriate portfolio.
18 points for moderate concentration with a clear reason.
10 points for a highly concentrated portfolio that is later improved.
0 points for deliberately increasing extreme concentration to chase growth.
deductions: Do not award extra points only for using every category.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: This measures dependence on one investment type, not simply the number of categories.

dimensions.label: Asset-Role Understanding
positiveRules: Four points for each correct asset-role match.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: This measures whether the learner understands ownership, lending, pooled investing, baskets, and cash.

dimensions.label: Profit and Trade-Off Understanding
positiveRules: Ten points for all four correct company-profit predictions.
Five points for choosing a final portfolio action that responds to the actual mismatch.
deductions: Deduct 5 for treating dividends as required or guaranteed.
dimensions.learnerExplanation: This measures whether company profit choices and portfolio adjustments are judged by context.

strengthRules.message: You matched the final allocation well to the selected timeline and cash need.
You reduced dependence on one investment type without treating diversification as risk-free.

The cash allocation may be too low for the amount that could be needed soon.
The portfolio’s price movement does not fit well with when the money may be needed.

tradeoffRules.message: You prioritised access and lower price movement, accepting lower long-term growth potential.
You accepted greater uncertainty for higher growth potential.
You reduced concentration, but every investment type can still lose value.

questions.question: Which portfolio decision combines time horizon, diversification, and cash access?

options.label: Choose the assets with the highest growth score
options.feedback: Growth potential alone does not show whether money is accessible or overly concentrated.

options.label: Spread money for clear roles while keeping suitable cash for the goal
options.feedback: Correct. The decision considers the whole portfolio and the goal.

options.label: Use every asset category equally
options.feedback: Equal allocations may ignore the timeline and why each category is included.

options.label: Keep no cash because it grows slowly
options.feedback: Cash may be useful when some money must remain accessible.

questions.correctExplanation: A strong portfolio connects the asset mix with the goal, timeline, concentration, and access need.
questions.misconceptionTested: A strong portfolio is simply the one with the highest possible growth potential.

questions.question: A portfolio contains shares in five technology companies. What can be concluded?

options.label: It is automatically well diversified
options.feedback: Several companies may still depend on the same industry and similar risks.

options.label: It may still be concentrated in one industry
options.feedback: Correct. The number of stocks does not fully describe diversification.

options.label: It cannot lose value because the companies are different
options.feedback: Different companies can still fall together or face similar pressures.

options.label: It must pay five dividends
options.feedback: Companies are not required to pay dividends.

questions.correctExplanation: Diversification considers industries, asset types, and dependence on shared outcomes—not just the number of names.
questions.misconceptionTested: Holding several individual stocks always creates a diversified portfolio.

questions.question: A goal is two years away, and part of the money may be needed suddenly. Which review matters most?

options.label: Whether the portfolio has the highest growth potential
options.feedback: The near-term goal and access need may make high price movement difficult.

options.label: Whether enough cash is accessible and price movement fits the timeline
options.feedback: Correct. Access and time-horizon alignment matter together.

options.label: Whether every company pays a dividend
options.feedback: Dividends are optional and do not solve every access or risk issue.

options.label: Whether all money is kept in individual stocks
options.feedback: A single high-movement category may create a mismatch for money needed soon.

questions.correctExplanation: Money needed within a shorter period should be reviewed for access and possible price movement.
questions.misconceptionTested: Cash has no useful portfolio role.
